paragraphs: Abductive learning connects a perception model with logical background knowledge. The reasoning component proposes explanations that satisfy the knowledge, and those explanations provide supervision for learning. The difficulty is that several explanations may fit the same rules. Logical compatibility therefore leaves ambiguity: the candidate set can contain both correct and incorrect answers.

Earlier approaches choose the candidate with the least inconsistency with the knowledge base. That decision can discard useful uncertainty and supply misleading supervision when the selected candidate is wrong. Ambiguity-Aware Abductive Learning instead evaluates all potential candidates together with their probabilities. Its central change is to use the ambiguous collection of explanations as learning information rather than immediately reduce it to one answer.

The paper reports experimental and theoretical support for substantial improvements over prior abductive learning. The stated benefit comes from exploiting supervision that remains uncertain, helping the perception model avoid suboptimal solutions caused by mistaken candidate selection. This makes handling ambiguity part of the learning procedure itself.
icml-2024-ambiguity-aware-abductive-lear.tldr: Ambiguity-Aware Abductive Learning improves learning from logical supervision by considering all candidate explanations and their probabilities.

paragraphs: Resonate-and-fire neurons are spiking neuron models whose internal dynamics resonate over time. This gives them a way to extract frequency patterns directly from temporal inputs. Although the model is simple and biologically plausible, earlier formulations have intrinsic shortcomings that interfere with learning and limit the usefulness of this frequency sensitivity.

The paper introduces balanced resonate-and-fire neurons, which alleviate some of those shortcomings. It evaluates networks built from these neurons on several sequence learning tasks. The focus is on whether the revised neuron dynamics can make recurrent spiking networks both effective at processing sequences and more economical in their use of spikes and parameters.

Across the reported comparisons, these networks achieve higher overall task performance while producing substantially fewer spikes and using fewer parameters than modern recurrent spiking networks. Training also converges faster and more stably, including when backpropagation spans hundreds of time steps. These findings support the architecture as a candidate for larger spiking networks and efficient hardware implementations; those future uses remain proposed directions.
icml-2024-balanced-resonate-and-fire-neu.tldr: Balanced resonate-and-fire neurons improve sequence learning in recurrent spiking networks while reducing spikes, parameters, and training difficulty.

paragraphs: BEYOND detects adversarial examples by examining how an input relates to augmented versions of itself. These versions form its neighborhood. The paper reports that clean inputs tend to remain similar to their neighbors in both internal representation and predicted label, whereas adversarial inputs exhibit larger discrepancies along these two dimensions.

The framework uses an existing self-supervised learning model to extract representations and predict labels. It turns representation similarity and label consistency into evidence for detecting an attack. This makes the relationship between an input and its own transformations central to the decision. The authors also provide an explanation and a rigorous justification for why this discrepancy is useful.

Experiments report stronger detection and greater speed than the compared baselines, with particularly large gains under adaptive attacks. BEYOND can also work alongside an adversarially trained classifier; the reported combination achieves state-of-the-art robustness accuracy. Together, these findings support self-supervised neighborhood relationships as a practical detection signal in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-be-your-own-neighborhood-detec.tldr: BEYOND detects adversarial inputs through inconsistencies between their self-supervised representations and labels and those of their augmented neighbors.

paragraphs: ΦFlow is a Python toolkit for writing simulations that support differentiation and integrate with PyTorch, TensorFlow, Jax, and NumPy. Its motivation is that scientific and engineering simulations need capabilities that general machine learning libraries do not primarily target. The toolkit supplies those capabilities while retaining the computational features of its underlying libraries.

Its tools include differential operators, boundary conditions, precision management, and code that works across different numbers of dimensions. It also provides differentiable preconditioned sparse linear solves, automatic matrix construction through function tracing, SciPy optimizer integration, simulation vectorization, and visualization. Together, these features address both the mathematical operations and the practical programming work involved in implementing simulations.

The resulting framework simplifies differential equation solvers on grids and unstructured meshes, with built-in support for fluid simulation. It retains automatic differentiation, just-in-time compilation, and GPU or TPU support through the base libraries. The abstract also reports use in research publications and as a ground-truth solver for scientific datasets, establishing applications beyond the toolkit's feature list.
icml-2024-bf-textrmflow-differentiable-s.tldr: ΦFlow adds scientific simulation tools to major numerical and machine learning libraries while retaining differentiation and hardware acceleration.

paragraphs: Different learning objectives can appear to express different preferences about model errors. This paper studies when those distinctions disappear at the optimum. It calls this phenomenon criterion collapse: optimizing one metric also produces an optimum for another. The main concern is collapse into solutions that minimize error probability, even when the chosen training criterion has a different form.

The analysis covers a broad collection of objectives, including distributionally robust optimization, optimized certainty equivalent risks, conditional value at risk, and tilted empirical risk minimization. It also considers non-monotonic criteria associated with Flooding and SoftAD. For Bernoulli-distributed losses, the paper establishes collapse results extending beyond previously studied cases involving conditional value at risk and distributional robustness.

The authors then examine surrogate losses and identify conditions under which monotonic criteria, including tilted empirical risk minimization, cannot escape collapse. Non-monotonic alternatives can avoid it. The contribution therefore clarifies when changing the learning criterion can meaningfully change the preferred solution, with the conclusions depending on the conditions established in the analysis.
icml-2024-criterion-collapse-and-loss-di.tldr: The paper identifies conditions where different learning criteria collapse into error-probability minimization and where non-monotonic alternatives can avoid that collapse.

paragraphs: Channel codes are designed to make communication more reliable in the presence of errors. This paper explores whether learning can automate part of their design, focusing on short-to-medium block lengths. Its starting point is polar coding, whose construction rests on a polarization kernel and which the abstract identifies as a leading approach in this regime.

DeepPolar extends that framework with larger kernels and a nonlinear construction. Neural networks parameterize both the kernels and their matched decoders. The learning problem therefore covers the coding components and the corresponding decoding components together. This preserves the polar-code framework while expanding the kinds of transformations that can be represented within it.

The reported results show that the learned codes make effective use of larger kernels and improve reliability over both existing neural codes and conventional polar codes. The finding supports this particular route to automated code design: combining an established coding structure with learned nonlinear components. The contribution is a demonstrated improvement within that design approach and the evaluated regime.
icml-2024-deeppolar-inventing-nonlinear-.tldr: DeepPolar learns nonlinear, larger-kernel polar codes and matched decoders that improve reported communication reliability over conventional polar and existing neural codes.

paragraphs: Differential privacy supports releasing learned models while protecting the data used to train them. A complication arises when the same training data is reused for further model releases: those releases incur additional privacy budget costs. Generating private synthetic data offers one possible response, but models trained on such data can perform worse than private models designed directly for a task.

This paper proposes a sum-product-network method that combines private classification and private data generation in one model. The same learned model can therefore serve a predictive role and a generative role. The authors describe this combination of discriminative and generative capabilities as, to their knowledge, a first for differentially private machine learning.

The reported comparisons show improvements over the state of the art in generated-data utility and training stability. Here stability specifically concerns the number of training runs needed for convergence. These findings matter because a reusable private model must produce useful outputs and train reliably; the proposed approach addresses both within a shared modeling framework.
icml-2024-differentially-private-sum-pro.tldr: A differentially private sum-product network supports both classification and synthetic data generation, with reported gains in training stability and generated-data utility.

paragraphs: Controlling a system with many actuators is difficult for reinforcement learning, especially when several actuators offer overlapping ways to produce movement. Musculoskeletal systems provide a motivating example. The paper draws on muscle synergies, a proposed biological mechanism in which coordinated actuator activity simplifies the generation of motor commands.

DynSyn derives coordinated actuator representations from a system's dynamical structure. It then adapts those representations to the task and the current state. This combines information about how the system moves with flexibility about what movement is needed now. The intended benefit is a more useful representation for learning control than treating the high-dimensional actuator space without this coordination.

Across tasks involving different musculoskeletal models, the authors report state-of-the-art sample efficiency and robustness relative to the tested baselines. They also find that the learned representations are interpretable, capture essential dynamical features, and generalize across diverse motor tasks. These results support using system dynamics to guide actuator coordination while allowing that coordination to change with the control situation.
icml-2024-dynsyn-dynamical-synergistic-r.tldr: DynSyn uses system dynamics to learn adaptable actuator coordination, improving reported learning efficiency and robustness in musculoskeletal control tasks.

paragraphs: Sampling without replacement reveals only part of a finite population. When that population contains multiple categories, both its total size and the number of elements in each category may be unknown. This paper addresses estimating those quantities using the multivariate hypergeometric distribution, whose likelihood reflects the sampling process directly.

The proposed method handles severe undersampling and also allows the underlying distribution to vary with a continuous latent variable. A variational autoencoder provides the framework for this latent structure. This lets the model account for data generated from a mixture of conditional distributions, a setting the authors connect to collaborative filtering, while estimating the hidden population quantities.

In simulations, the method outperforms other count-data likelihoods in population-size estimation and in learning an informative latent space. Applications illustrate two uses: estimating the complexity of latent vocabularies from reading excerpts and recovering gene-transcript counts from sparse single-cell genomics data. The results connect the choice of sampling likelihood with both better size estimates and useful learned representations.
icml-2024-estimating-unknown-population-.tldr: A hypergeometric likelihood within a variational autoencoder estimates unknown population and category sizes from severely undersampled data.

paragraphs: The paper studies transformers that show little learning progress for hundreds of epochs and then improve abruptly. On the examined multi-step tasks, the prolonged plateau is associated with difficulty learning an intermediate task. Once that intermediate task is learned, both the apparent understanding of the problem and the loss can change rapidly.

The authors design synthetic tasks to investigate these transitions, which they call Eureka-moments. Similar performance leaps also occur in language modeling and in-context learning. They suspect that the multi-step nature of these problems contributes to the transitions. In the synthetic setting, they trace the optimization difficulty to the softmax function inside self-attention and identify ways to alleviate it.

The proposed fixes reduce training steps, increase the likelihood of learning the intermediate task, improve final accuracy, and reduce sensitivity to hyperparameters in the reported work. Improvements developed on the synthetic tasks also help language modeling and in-context learning. The results link a controlled optimization diagnosis to useful training changes without establishing that every abrupt learning transition has the same cause.
icml-2024-eureka-moments-in-transformers.tldr: Synthetic multi-step tasks reveal softmax-related transformer training difficulties, and targeted fixes also improve language modeling and in-context learning.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning helps language models follow requests and human preferences, making them more useful for programming. The paper identifies a gap in that process: existing tuning schemes overlook the security of the code they generate. Consequently, even highly capable instruction-tuned models frequently produce unsafe code, despite their practical usefulness.

SafeCoder incorporates security into fine-tuning. The authors build an automated pipeline to collect a diverse, high-quality dataset for this purpose, then combine security-focused training with ordinary instruction tuning. The design treats security and utility as joint training objectives. This matters because improving code safety should be evaluated alongside the model's ability to remain useful to the person requesting code.

Across several popular language models and datasets, the authors report an approximately 30% improvement in security while preserving utility. The abstract does not specify a more detailed interpretation of that percentage. The main finding is that this relatively simple combined training procedure improves the reported security outcome without sacrificing the usefulness measured in the evaluations.
icml-2024-instruction-tuning-for-secure-.tldr: SafeCoder combines security-focused and standard instruction tuning, reporting about 30% better code security while preserving utility.

paragraphs: Offline design optimization uses existing observations to search for better designs when new experiments are expensive. A surrogate model predicts the objective for candidate designs and guides that search. The difficulty is that its predictions can become inaccurate beyond the observed data, so a design that looks excellent to the surrogate may fall short under the true objective.

The paper develops a theoretical framework connecting surrogate error to optimization quality. Its bound depends on how closely the surrogate matches the underlying gradient field: the pattern of directions in which the true objective changes. This provides a way to analyze the gap between optimizing the learned model and reaching the true optimum.

Motivated by that analysis, the authors propose a black-box gradient-matching algorithm for training surrogates. They report improvements over previous approaches on multiple real-world benchmarks. The contribution connects a theoretical measure of what makes a surrogate useful for optimization with a training method designed around that measure, rather than relying solely on the surrogate's predicted objective values.
icml-2024-learning-surrogates-for-offlin.tldr: The paper bounds offline optimization quality through gradient-field matching and uses that analysis to train better surrogate models.

paragraphs: An RNN's weight matrix determines how it processes sequences, but turning those weights into a useful description of its behavior is challenging. This paper compares two perspectives. Mechanistic methods inspect the weights directly, while functionalist methods study the input-output behavior that those weights produce.

The authors examine several mechanistic approaches and adapt a permutation-equivariant Deep Weight Space layer to recurrent networks. They also introduce two functionalist methods that probe an RNN with inputs and encode information from its responses. A theoretical framework establishes conditions under which these behavioral probes can produce rich representations useful for determining how the RNN behaves.

For evaluation, the paper introduces two RNN model-zoo datasets: formal-language generators and classifiers that process MNIST digits sequentially. An emulation-based self-supervised technique supports comparisons across downstream applications. Functionalist methods clearly outperform the alternatives on the hardest reported task, identifying the exact task used to train an RNN. This finding gives behavioral probing a particularly strong role in recovering information about a network's training task.
icml-2024-learning-useful-representation.tldr: Probing RNN behavior produces useful weight representations and clearly improves identification of training tasks in the paper's hardest evaluation.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can provide prior knowledge about clean signals for Bayesian denoising. However, diffusion-based posterior sampling ordinarily requires the noise level and covariance to be known. Blind denoising must infer those noise properties as well as the clean signal, so treating them as fixed inputs leaves an important part of the problem unresolved.

Gibbs Diffusion addresses this by alternating between two sampling steps. A conditional diffusion model samples the signal, while a Monte Carlo sampler infers the noise parameters. The method assumes a parametric Gaussian noise model. Within that setting, it targets joint posterior inference over the signal and the parameters describing its corruption.

The theoretical analysis identifies potential pitfalls, informs diagnostics, and quantifies how diffusion-model errors affect the Gibbs stationary distribution. Demonstrations include natural images with colored noise of unknown amplitude and exponent, and cosmic microwave background analysis. In the cosmology application, inferring the quantities treated as noise parameters constrains models of the Universe's evolution, making noise estimation itself scientifically meaningful.
icml-2024-listening-to-the-noise-blind-d.tldr: Gibbs Diffusion alternates signal and noise-parameter sampling to enable blind denoising under parametric Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: Dynamical systems reconstruction seeks a generative model of an underlying process from time-series measurements. Compact models are valuable, but the paper finds that removing small neural-network weights is ineffective for this task. Even a connection with a small weight can make a substantial contribution to the dynamics the model must reproduce.

The proposed alternative is geometric pruning. It removes connections according to their contribution to an attractor's geometrical structure, using their effect on the reconstructed dynamics to judge importance. The authors report that this approach substantially reduces parameter counts without significantly degrading reconstruction quality. It therefore offers a way to simplify the network while retaining its important dynamical behavior.

The pruned networks exhibit a particular topology, and the paper finds that this connectivity pattern matters more to performance than weight magnitudes. The authors provide an algorithm to generate such topologies as priors for recurrent generative models. Comparisons with small-world and scale-free networks investigate how this structure relates to other established patterns of connectivity.
icml-2024-optimal-recurrent-network-topo.tldr: Pruning recurrent networks by their contribution to attractor geometry yields compact dynamical models and reveals useful connectivity patterns.

paragraphs: This position paper asks how machine learning fits the goals and practices of natural science. The authors characterize ML as emphasizing data and judging models through performance on held-out data. They argue that these commitments can conflict with scientific approaches concerned with physical explanations and other standards of knowledge.

The paper identifies settings where ML's flexibility is valuable. In causal inference, expressive models can represent confounding effects such as foregrounds, backgrounds, and instrument calibration parameters. The authors argue that using model capacity for these effects can make scientific results more trustworthy. The usefulness of ML therefore depends partly on the role it plays within the inference.

The authors also identify harmful uses: emulating physical simulations can amplify confirmation bias, and labels produced by expressive regressions can introduce uncontrolled bias in downstream joint or ensemble analyses. Their answers come from a physics perspective and are explicitly partial. The broader invitation is for scientific communities to examine how ML changes the meaning and reliability of their conclusions.
icml-2024-position-is-machine-learning-g.tldr: From a physics perspective, this position paper explains how ML can strengthen scientific inference in some roles and introduce serious biases in others.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges how empirical machine learning research understands its own results. The authors argue that a common but incomplete view of experimentation contributes to findings that cannot be replicated and conclusions that are unreliable. They present this as a threat to progress because later research depends on what earlier experiments appear to establish.

The central distinction is between exploratory and confirmatory research. Exploration helps develop possible explanations and directions for investigation; confirmation presents evidence as testing a claim. The authors argue that much current empirical ML work is presented in the second category even though it should be understood in the first. Their concern is therefore about the interpretation and status of experimental knowledge.

The proposed response is greater awareness of the different ways experiments can contribute knowledge, together with their epistemic limits. Recognizing research as exploratory changes the strength of the conclusions it can support. The paper's contribution is a methodological argument for aligning claims with the kind of evidence the research actually provides.
icml-2024-position-why-we-must-rethink-e.tldr: The authors argue that much empirical ML research should be treated as exploratory and that miscasting it as confirmatory undermines reliability.

paragraphs: Partial monitoring describes sequential decisions where an agent sees only an incomplete signal about what happened. The agent must use those signals to reduce cumulative loss even though the outcomes and losses themselves are unobserved. In the contextual version, additional information is available before acting and helps determine the distribution of outcomes.

The paper studies both contextual and non-contextual settings with stochastic outcomes. It introduces strategies that randomize otherwise deterministic confidence bounds, producing the RandCBP and RandCBPside* methods. It also extends regret guarantees to settings where existing stochastic strategies do not apply. These guarantees address learning performance despite the restricted feedback available to the agent.

Experiments across several partial-monitoring games show performance competitive with state-of-the-art baselines. The authors also design a use case for monitoring the error rate of a deployed classifier. That example illustrates how the framework can describe a practical monitoring problem in which the information needed to evaluate a system is only partially available.
icml-2024-randomized-confidence-bounds-f.tldr: Randomized confidence bounds yield competitive partial-monitoring strategies and extend regret guarantees to additional stochastic settings.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains a shared model using a weighted combination of task losses. Adaptive weighting often gives more attention to tasks with larger losses. Label noise complicates this strategy: a noisy task can retain a high loss even at its best achievable performance, attracting excessive weight and reducing performance on other tasks.

ExcessMTL balances tasks according to estimated distance from convergence. It assigns greater weight to tasks that are less fully trained, separating remaining learning opportunity from loss that may reflect noise. To make this practical, the authors develop a Taylor-approximation method for estimating excess risks, described as both efficient and accurate.

The theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees and Pareto stationarity, a multi-objective stationarity property relevant to balancing tasks. Experiments on several multi-task benchmarks show stronger performance than existing methods when label noise is present. The findings support weighting tasks by how much learning remains, addressing the specific failure mode in which persistently noisy tasks dominate training.
icml-2024-robust-multi-task-learning-wit.tldr: ExcessMTL weights tasks by estimated distance from convergence, improving multi-task learning when label noise makes raw losses misleading.

paragraphs: Many deep reinforcement learning methods optimize discounted reward, giving different weight to rewards depending on how far into the future they occur. For continuing tasks, this objective can differ from the performance measure of interest. The paper develops an approach based on average reward to address that possible mismatch.

RVI-SAC extends Soft Actor-Critic to the average-reward setting. Its critic updates use RVI Q-learning, while its actor updates follow an average-reward soft policy improvement theorem. These changes adapt both the estimation of action quality and the improvement of the policy to the chosen objective. The method also automatically adjusts a Reset Cost so that average-reward learning can be applied to tasks with termination.

The authors evaluate RVI-SAC on Gymnasium MuJoCo locomotion tasks and report competitive performance against existing methods. The result supports the feasibility of average-reward, off-policy deep reinforcement learning in those evaluations. Its main contribution is an adaptation of a strong existing method to an objective motivated by continuing-task performance.
icml-2024-rvi-sac-average-reward-off-pol.tldr: RVI-SAC adapts Soft Actor-Critic to average reward and reports competitive performance on MuJoCo locomotion tasks.

paragraphs: Fast convolution methods reduce computation, but their numerical precision requirements can conflict with model quantization. SFC addresses this tension with an algebraic transform that extends the discrete Fourier transform using symbolic computation. At selected transform points, the transformation requires only additions, avoiding irrational-number calculations and lowering the precision requirement.

The method also introduces correction terms that turn otherwise invalid circular-convolution outputs into usable results. This improves how much useful computation the Fourier approach delivers. Numerical error analysis connects these algorithmic changes to the balance between reducing multiplication counts and keeping errors small, which is central when arithmetic uses limited precision.

For 3×3 convolution, the paper establishes a 3.68-fold multiplication reduction, compared with a 2.25-fold reduction for Winograd at similarly low numerical error. These figures concern multiplication counts. Benchmark and FPGA experiments additionally report improved computational efficiency while maintaining accuracy, surpassing quantization alone and existing fast-convolution quantization approaches. The findings support designing the transform itself around low-precision arithmetic.
icml-2024-sfc-achieve-accurate-fast-conv.tldr: SFC redesigns Fourier-based convolution for low precision, reducing multiplication counts and improving reported efficiency while maintaining accuracy.

paragraphs: Sparse Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms reduce dimensionality while approximately preserving every pairwise distance among a set of points. Their computational cost depends on how many nonzero entries each projection-matrix column contains. Fewer entries mean less work when applying the transform, making matrix sparsity an important target even when the output dimension is already near optimal.

Existing upper and lower bounds suggest limited room for improvement, but the cited lower bound assumes the original dimension is at least proportional to the number of points. This paper revisits the problem when the dimension grows subpolynomially with that number. It provides a sparser embedding in that regime, retaining the stated distance-preservation and output-dimension goals.

The authors also strengthen the lower bound so that it applies when the dimension is much smaller than the number of points. This matches the first term of their new sparsity upper bound. A further result improves sparsity for oblivious subspace embeddings at optimal output dimension. Together, the results refine how attainable sparsity depends on the dimensional regime.
icml-2024-sparse-dimensionality-reductio.tldr: The paper improves sparse dimensionality reduction when input dimension grows subpolynomially with the number of points and strengthens complementary lower bounds.

paragraphs: Some biologically motivated learning algorithms represent gradients through differences in neural activity. Many require separate synchronized learning phases or extremely small output perturbations, creating computational overhead and difficulties in noisy settings. Dual propagation addresses these issues using artificial neurons with two compartments that receive opposite nudges.

Prior work showed that this fully local algorithm can bridge the performance gap to backpropagation without separate phases or infinitesimal perturbations. However, its numerical stability depends on symmetric nudging. That requirement can be restrictive for biological interpretations and analog implementations, where the symmetry of the two perturbations is a relevant constraint.

This paper provides a firmer foundation for the objective behind dual propagation and uncovers a connection to adversarial robustness. It also relates dual propagation to a particular adjoint-state method that remains stable with asymmetric nudging. These contributions clarify what the algorithm optimizes and connect it to a method that relaxes its symmetry-dependent stability requirement, directly addressing a stated obstacle to implementation.
icml-2024-two-tales-of-single-phase-cont.tldr: The paper grounds dual propagation's objective and connects it to an adjoint-state method that stays stable under asymmetric nudging.

paragraphs: Score-based diffusion models can generate images using stochastic sampling or deterministic probability-flow differential equations. These sampling choices can differ in performance, and the paper seeks a mathematical framework for understanding that disparity. It introduces a formulation based on Feynman's path integral, a technique originating in quantum physics.

Within this formulation, the authors derive backward stochastic differential equations and loss functions for diffusion models. A parameter connects the stochastic and deterministic sampling schemes, allowing both to be studied within the same description. The paper identifies this parameter as analogous to Planck's constant, establishing a mathematical connection that makes tools from quantum physics applicable.

The authors use that connection to apply the Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin expansion when evaluating negative log-likelihood. This supplies a way to assess the performance difference between the sampling schemes. The contribution is a unified analytical viewpoint and an associated approximation technique for studying diffusion sampling, with the physics analogy serving as a route to the mathematical analysis.
icml-2024-understanding-diffusion-models.tldr: A path-integral formulation connects stochastic and deterministic diffusion sampling and enables a quantum-physics approximation for analyzing their performance difference.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational approach to robustness certification for message-passing neural networks with ReLU activations. Certification concerns whether a network can be trusted under a specified collection of allowed changes. The method uses mixed-integer optimization to represent the network and the perturbations considered by the verification problem.

The formulation can accommodate added and removed edges, global and local perturbation budgets, and changes to both topology and features. Its central technique uses graph structure to tighten variable bounds within the optimization. The authors also investigate more aggressive tightening that dynamically updates constraints as variable bounds improve, aiming to make the verification computation more effective.

The approach is implemented as an extension to the open-source SCIP branch-and-cut solver. Experiments cover node classification and graph classification, with topological attacks that can both add and remove edges. The contribution combines a flexible representation of verification problems with graph-aware tightening strategies, and evaluates those strategies on both levels of graph prediction.
icml-2024-verifying-message-passing-neur.tldr: Graph-structure-based bound tightening supports mixed-integer robustness verification of ReLU message-passing networks under specified perturbations.
